chk_problem.label: accurate
chk_problem.poster_evidence: The construction industry remains one of the least automated sectors, despite its economic scale and high-risk tasks—especially on roofs. Roof work involves hazardous conditions like falls and repetitive physical labor, making it ideal for robotic automation. Quadruped robots, while increasingly capable, remain underutilized in real-world applications. This work investigates whether commercial quadrupeds like the Unitree Go2 can operate effectively on tiled roofs—a novel, unexplored environment combining steep inclines, smooth surfaces, and discrete structural features.
chk_problem.reason: The poster accurately describes the research problem and motivation, focusing on the feasibility of using quadruped robots for roof environments and highlighting the hazards and repetitive tasks involved.

chk_method.label: accurate
chk_method.poster_evidence: A custom test rig simulating a German-style tiled roof (Frankfurther Pfanne) was built to evaluate the Unitree Go2’s performance. Three core locomotion tasks were tested: balancing on increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences in multiple orientations, and incline walking. Motion capture (OptiTrack) tracked foot slippage via reflective markers. Friction coefficients were measured using a UR10e force-torque sensor. All trials were automated via Python using WebRTC, with the robot set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.
chk_method.reason: The poster provides a clear description of the method, including the test rig design, the tasks evaluated, and the tools used for measurement, matching the reference.

chk_primary_result.label: accurate
chk_primary_result.poster_evidence: The Go2 failed to meet manufacturer claims of 40° slope capability. Standing balance failed at 27.58° ± 0.72°, primarily due to front-limb slippage. Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down) and 7° (sideways), failing when the center of mass exited the support polygon. Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001), with critical failures occurring regularly at 25°. Even on flat ground, tile steps caused slippage. Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance and no significant correlation with trajectory deviation. Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat) and 1.430 (curved), suggesting theoretical inclines >48°, but dynamic performance fell far short—highlighting control and stability as key bottlenecks.
chk_primary_result.reason: The poster accurately reports the primary result, including the quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle and critical failures at 25°, as well as the friction coefficients and their implications.
